summary:
Understanding global wildfire and agricultural fire dynamics requires decades of consistent satellite observations. However, NASAs two primary active-fire sensors—MODIS (operating since 2000 at 1 km resolution) and VIIRS (operating since 2012 at 375 m resolution)—cannot be compared directly, creating artificial count jumps that obscure real fire trends.

To solve this, Project Harmonized active-fire calendar developed an interactive web application that unifies MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m FIRMS records into a single, seamless timeline. Our pipeline maps detections onto a common 1 km grid, calibrates pre-2012 MODIS counts against VIIRS using origin regression during their overlap period, and computes daily climatologies. By highlighting critical fire periods, statistical anomalies, and fire season boundaries (onset, peak, and end), our tool empowers emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to anticipate severe fire activity and allocate resources effectively.
details:
What It Does And How It Works Developed by Project Harmonized active-fire calendar, this web-based analytical tool merges incompatible satellite hotspot datasets (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m) into one coherent daily and multi-year fire activity record for any user-selected Area of Interest (AOI). The application processes NASA FIRMS CSV records through a five-stage pipeline:

  1. Normalization: Aligns data fields and maps numeric MODIS confidence (0 to 100) and categorical VIIRS confidence (low, nominal, high) onto a unified scale.
  2. Spatial Gridding: Aggregates detections into unique cell-days on a configurable common grid (0.01 to 0.05 degrees, approximately 1 km) so multi-pixel VIIRS detections of a single fire match MODIS spatial footprints.
  3. Overlap Calibration: Fits a linear regression through the origin using weekly unique cell sums from 2012 onward, reporting both scaling factor and goodness-of-fit.
  4. Series Harmonization: Applies the scaling factor to historical records prior to 2012 and retains VIIRS as the modern baseline.
  5. Climatology And Anomaly Detection: Computes a centered 7-day smoothed series and day-of-year climatology across all years to flag critical days, critical periods, unusual days, and fire season milestones.

Benefits And Expected Impact

  • Early Warning And Emergency Response: Rapidly identifies whether current weekly fire activity is statistically abnormal compared to historical baselines.
  • Climate And Environmental Science: Provides an uninterrupted 25+ year record (2000 to present) free from sensor-transition artifacts for trend analysis.
  • Land And Resource Management: Pinpoints shifts in fire season onset, peak, and duration to optimize crew deployment and monitoring schedules.

Tools, Data And Technologies Used

  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active-fire datasets, plus built-in simulated demo datasets.
  • Software And Stack: Interactive web application built with HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and statistical data visualization components for calendar heatmaps, spatial hotspot mapping, and time-series regression charts.

Creativity And Key Considerations Rather than treating sensor differences as a barrier, we bridge two distinct orbital eras using transparent local calibration diagnostics. Our team carefully accounted for scientific transparency and operational limits: warning users when a single regional factor yields low correlation, noting differences in satellite overpass times, and clarifying that active-fire counts serve as a relative activity indicator rather than an exact burned-area measurement.
